passage: Zubin, my classmate at college, asked if he could join our Ganesh aarti, and I was curious how it would go. He arrived on time, left his shoes at the door and stood at the back with his hands loosely together, watching. He asked my mother quietly whether it was fine to take a photo of the idol. She said there was no need, and he nodded. When the aarti ended he took the prasad in his right hand, said thank you and asked what the modak stood for. My mother explained. He listened, asked one more question and told us about the fire temple where his family goes for Navroz. I can't say what he felt inside, but he looked interested, not pretending. At the door he said, "Thank you for letting me see it." Shreya

qa.q: What did Zubin ask after the aarti ended?
qa.a: Zubin asked what the modak stood for.

qa.q: What does Zubin's behaviour suggest he feels, and how sure can Shreya be?
qa.a: He seems interested and respectful, but Shreya cannot be certain of his inner state. Shreya only reads it from how he asked and listened.

qa.q: Which choices by Zubin showed respectful curiosity?
qa.a: He arrived on time, left his shoes at the door, stood at the back, asked before taking a photo, thanked the family and asked questions without pretending belief.

qa.q: How might Shreya's mother have felt answering Zubin's questions?
qa.a: Probably welcoming and glad to explain, since she answered patiently and told him there was no need for a photo.

grounding: A young adult attends a friend's family prayer to learn, asking respectfully and following local etiquette without any wish to change belief.

passage: Saturday. Avni asked her friend Asif, "Could I come to your family's iftar next week and watch the evening prayer? I want to learn, not to join." Asif smiled. "Ask Ammi, she'll be happy. Bring a dupatta for your head and leave your shoes outside." Wednesday. At Asif's home the family laid out the prayer mats. Avni sat quietly on a chair by the wall, head covered, and took no photos. Afterwards she asked Asif's mother, "Would it be all right to ask what you say?" and listened carefully to the answer. She ate dates and did not pretend to pray. Friday. Avni texted Asif: "Thank you. I felt welcome. I'm still myself, but I understand a little more."

qa.q: On which day did Avni ask Asif about the iftar?
qa.a: Avni asked Asif on Saturday.

qa.q: How does Avni seem to feel by Friday?
qa.a: Avni feels welcome and grateful. Avni thanks Asif and says, "I'm still myself, but I understand a little more."

qa.q: Which choice by Avni at Asif's home showed respect without pretending?
qa.a: She sat quietly with her head covered, took no photos, asked politely what was said, and did not pretend to pray.

qa.q: How might Asif's mother have felt when Avni asked what she says?
qa.a: Probably pleased and respected, since Avni asked politely and listened carefully to the answer.

passage:
Last December, Jomon invited me to midnight mass at his church in Kochi. I'm Pradeep, and I'd never been inside a church in my life. I was curious, and a little nervous about doing something wrong.
Before we went, I asked him, "What should I not do?" He laughed and said, "Don't take communion, just sit, and stand when we stand." I wore a plain shirt and left my phone on silent.
Inside, the candles and the choir were beautiful. I didn't know the words, so I just listened. At one point an old lady handed me her hymn book, open to the right page. I thanked her with a nod.
Afterwards, over plum cake at Jomon's house, I asked his father about why the carols mattered to him. He talked for an hour.
I'm still who I was. But I understand Jomon a little more.

qa.q: What did Jomon tell Pradeep not to do?
qa.a: Jomon said, "Don't take communion, just sit, and stand when we stand."

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel before going to the mass?
qa.a: Pradeep felt curious and a little nervous about doing something wrong.

qa.q: What made Pradeep's visit respectful?
qa.a: Pradeep asked about etiquette beforehand, dressed plainly, silenced the phone, followed the congregation, and asked Jomon's father questions afterward with real interest.

qa.q: How might Jomon's father feel when Pradeep asks about the carols?
qa.a: He would likely feel pleased and respected that his son's friend was genuinely interested, which is why he talked for an hour.

grounding: A young adult attends a friend's service to learn, asks about etiquette and honours the difference, without any wish to change belief.

passage:
Faculty note, comparative religion elective, field visit, Saturday.
We visited the Buddhist vihara where Kalyani's family has been going for years. Kalyani offered to guide the class.
Dhruv, 20, stayed close to her the whole visit. Before entering, he asked her quietly whether he should remove his shoes and whether he could sit on the mats. When the monks began chanting, he sat still with his hands folded, as Kalyani did, and did not take photos, though several others did.
Afterwards he asked a monk, politely, what the chant meant and why people bowed three times. He listened without arguing. On the bus back, he told Kalyani, "I don't think I'd ever follow it, but I get why it matters to you." She smiled.
Next step: I will ask Dhruv and Kalyani to lead a short discussion next week on visiting another faith's space respectfully.

qa.q: Where did the class visit?
qa.a: The class visited the Buddhist vihara where Kalyani's family has been going for years.

qa.q: What might Dhruv have been feeling when he asked Kalyani quietly about shoes and mats?
qa.a: Dhruv was probably curious and careful, anxious not to offend anyone in a sacred space.

qa.q: What in Dhruv's behaviour could others copy?
qa.a: He asked about etiquette first, didn't take photos, sat as others did, asked questions politely and listened without arguing.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel when Dhruv says he gets why it matters to her?
qa.a: Kalyani likely feels respected and happy that her friend honoured her tradition without pretending to share it.

grounding: A note records a young adult attending a friend's place of worship to learn, following etiquette and asking respectfully without wishing to convert.

passage:
Sunday night
Went with Swati and her family to the Jain temple for Paryushan today. First time.
I was nervous. Swati had told me: no leather, no food inside, don't touch the idols, wash hands and feet first. I borrowed cloth shoes from my brother and kept my wallet at home.
Inside, it was quiet and white and smelled of sandalwood. Swati's grandmother was doing a long prayer, and I just sat at the back. I didn't understand the words, but I understood the stillness.
Afterwards I asked Swati's grandmother why they say sorry to everyone during Paryushan. She said, "Michchhami Dukkadam. We ask forgiveness for any hurt, even ones we don't know we caused." I found that beautiful.
I'm not becoming Jain. Swati knows that, and her family didn't ask me to. I just wanted to understand her better, and I think I do.
Vikas

qa.q: What did Swati tell Vikas not to wear or bring?
qa.a: Swati said no leather, no food inside, don't touch the idols, and wash hands and feet first.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel sitting at the back during the prayer?
qa.a: Vikas felt nervous at first and then calm and moved by the stillness, even without understanding the words.

qa.q: Why is Vikas's approach a good model for visiting another faith?
qa.a: Vikas prepared by learning the rules, stayed respectful and quiet, and asked a genuine question afterwards, all without any aim of changing belief.

qa.q: How might Swati's grandmother see Vikas's question?
qa.a: She probably felt pleased and warm that a young visitor wanted to understand the meaning of Paryushan.

grounding: A young adult visits a friend's temple to learn, follows local etiquette and asks respectfully, without wishing to change belief.
